# Feistel network cipher for sequential IDs

> A 4-round Feistel network using HMAC-SHA256 creates a one-to-one mapping from sequential 40-bit IDs to random-looking numbers and back.

_Part of [Turn sequential ids into random-looking codes](feistel-code-scrambler.md)_

When sequential IDs are exposed (link IDs 1, 2, 3, ...), attackers can enumerate all links by guessing. This cipher prevents that by encrypting IDs into random-looking codes using a Feistel network. The 40-bit ID is split into two 20-bit halves; for 4 rounds, each round applies `round` (HMAC-SHA256 of the round number and the right half) and XORs it with the left half, then swaps the halves. A Feistel network is a mathematical bijection—every ID maps to exactly one unique code—so no collisions occur and no collision checking is needed. The scrambled number is encoded as 7 base-62 characters (0-9A-Za-z) via [`toBase62`](share-short-links.md), creating a short random-looking code. To reverse it, [`unscramble`](share-short-links.md) runs the rounds in reverse order, undoing the encryption to recover the original ID. This reversibility is essential: when you need to recover the ID from a code (like looking up link details), the same key and algorithm decrypt it perfectly.

**Look at:** [`scramble` in codes.ts](../../../../packages/backend/libs/domains/marketing/domain/codes.ts#L34) · [`unscramble` in codes.ts](../../../../packages/backend/libs/domains/marketing/domain/codes.ts#L47) · [`round` in codes.ts](../../../../packages/backend/libs/domains/marketing/domain/codes.ts#L28)

## Pieces

- 40-bit ID space and 4-round Feistel network configuration: `HALF_BITS = 20` splits the ID into two 20-bit halves (1.1 trillion possible codes, fitting in 62^7); `ROUNDS = 4` provides the rounds for cryptographic strength.
- Decrypt a scrambled number back to the original ID: `unscramble(value, key)` runs the 4 Feistel rounds in reverse order (from round 3 down to 0) with the same key to undo the encryption and recover the original ID.
- One round of HMAC-SHA256-based mixing: `round(key, r, half)` computes HMAC-SHA256 of the key and the string `r:half`, masks the result to 20 bits, and returns it to be XORed with the other half.

## Watch out

- IDs must fit in exactly 40 bits (0 to 1,099,511,627,775); passing an ID outside this range throws a `RangeError` immediately.
- The `key` parameter completely determines the output: the same ID with different keys produces completely different codes, so the key must be consistent and kept secret like any cryptographic key.
- A Feistel network is always a bijection, so every ID maps to exactly one unique code—no collisions occur, which is why there's no collision checking or retry loop in the code.
- You cannot reverse a scrambled code to its ID without the key and the original algorithm; to an attacker with only the code it's one-way, but with the key it's perfectly reversible.
